chapter.title: Meet the builder: the terminal and your first request

cards.body: Your first working program is about three sentences away, and none of them are code. Claude Code is a builder you've hired, and the *terminal*, a plain text window where you type instead of click, is the site office where you meet them. **You pick the plot (a folder), call the builder in, and say what you want in plain English.**
cards.simpler: You can have a working program in about three sentences, and none of them are code. Think of Claude Code as a builder you have hired. The terminal is a plain window where you type instead of click. It is the site office where you meet the builder. **You pick a folder for the plot, call the builder in, and say what you want in plain English.**

cards.prompt: Maya wants a tiny page that says hello. She has the terminal open. Where should she be standing before she calls the builder in?

options.text: In a new, empty folder she made just for this project
Wherever the terminal happens to open; Claude will work out where to build
Inside the folder where Claude Code itself got installed

whyNot.b: That's the terminal's default spot, not your plot: Claude only builds inside the folder it was started in, so you choose the folder first.
whyNot.c: That's the builder's own toolbox, not your house: where Claude Code is installed and where your project lives are two different folders.

cards.reteach: Claude Code treats the folder you start it in as the whole job site. Files it writes land there, and it reads what's already there. So make a fresh folder for each project, step into it, and start Claude from inside it.

cards.title: The site office
cards.body:
The terminal is a window that only understands typed commands, one per line, Enter after each. On a Mac it's the app called Terminal. It looks bare. That's fine.

Three commands walk you to the plot. Typing mkdir hello-site makes a folder named hello-site. Typing cd hello-site steps inside it (*cd* means change directory, an older word for folder). Typing claude calls the builder in, and a welcome box appears.

**From the welcome box on, what you type is English for Claude, not a command for the terminal.** Installing is one line copied from Anthropic's Claude Code install page, done once.
cards.simpler: The terminal only understands typed commands, one per line, Enter after each. On a Mac it is the app called Terminal. Type mkdir hello-site to make a folder. Type cd hello-site to step inside it; cd means change directory. Type claude to call the builder in, and a welcome box appears. **From then on you are talking to Claude in English, not typing commands for the terminal.** Installing is one line from Anthropic's install page, done once.

cards.title: Priya's green morning
cards.body: Priya makes a folder called hello-site, steps into it and types claude. She writes: 'Make one web page that says Good morning, Priya in big green letters, and open it in my browser.' Claude says it will create a file called index.html, asks permission to run the command that opens it, and she presses yes. Her browser pops up with the greeting about 90 seconds after she started, in **a green that could stop traffic**. She types 'Navy instead,' and the same file changes colour in 10 seconds.
cards.simpler: Priya makes a folder called hello-site, steps inside and types claude. She asks for a page saying Good morning, Priya in big green letters, opened in her browser. Claude says it will make a file called index.html, then asks permission to open it. She presses yes. Ninety seconds after she started, her browser pops up with the greeting in **a green that could stop traffic**. She types 'Navy instead,' and the same file changes colour in 10 seconds.

cards.prompt: Dev has the welcome box open inside a fresh folder. Which first request fits the builder's first visit?

options.text: Make a page with one button that counts how many times I click it, and open it in my browser.
Build me a booking system for my aunt's salon, with payments.

whyNot.b: That's the whole house, not the first brick: a small, visible job proves the builder works before you trust them with the big one. Chapter 6 splits big ideas up.
whyNot.c: That's a shrug, not a brief: Claude can't show you something working if you haven't said what working looks like.

cards.reteach: The first request should be small enough to finish in minutes and visible enough that you can see it run: a page, a button, a colour. You are checking that the folder, the builder and the browser all connect. Big asks come later, in pieces.

cards.title: Yes, in my folder
cards.body:
Before Claude writes a file or runs a command, it asks. You'd expect a builder to barge in; this one holds up the plan and waits. Read the one line it shows. If it names something inside your project folder, press yes. If it wants to touch something elsewhere on your computer, pause and ask it why first.

'Open it in my browser' is the part people skip. **Asking to see it run turns a file into proof.** Then keep talking: 'bigger text', 'add a second line', 'navy'. Each reply edits the same file, so the page in your browser keeps catching up with you.
cards.simpler: Before Claude writes a file or runs a command, it asks. Read the one line it shows. If it names something inside your project folder, press yes. If it wants to touch anything outside that folder, stop and ask why. Most people skip 'open it in my browser'. Don't. **Asking to see it run turns a file into proof.** Then keep talking: 'bigger text', 'navy'. Each reply edits the same file, so your browser page keeps catching up with you.

cards.body: Tomás opens the terminal, types 'make a page that says hi' and gets back: command not found: make. He decides Claude Code is broken and closes the window. He never typed claude, so he was speaking English to the terminal, which only knows commands, and it grabbed his first word and went looking for a tool called make. **Spot it by the welcome box: no box, no builder.**
cards.simpler: Tomás opens the terminal and types 'make a page that says hi'. The terminal answers: command not found: make. He decides Claude Code is broken and closes the window. The real problem is that he never typed claude. He was speaking English to the terminal, which only knows commands. It grabbed his first word and went looking for a tool called make. **Spot it by the welcome box: no box, no builder.**

cards.prompt: Sam types 'build a page that shows the time' and the terminal answers: command not found: build. What happened?

options.text: Sam spoke English to the terminal before typing claude, so it tried to run the first word as a command
Sam was in the wrong folder, so Claude couldn't find the project

whyNot.a: That's a guess the message doesn't support: the terminal understood Sam fine, it just treated 'build' as a tool name. An install problem would show up when typing claude itself.
whyNot.c: That's the plot problem, not the language problem: a wrong folder puts files in the wrong place, it doesn't produce command not found.

cards.reteach: Two listeners share one window. The terminal hears commands like cd and claude. Claude hears English. Until the welcome box appears, the terminal is the one listening, and it will try to run your first word as a command.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body:
Open the terminal, make a folder for the project, step inside it, type claude. Then ask in plain English for **one small thing you can see run**, and press yes when it asks to work inside your folder.

Tomorrow: why 'make it better' is the worst instruction you can give a builder.
cards.simpler: Open the terminal. Make a folder for the project and step inside it. Type claude. Then ask, in plain English, for **one small thing you can see run**. When Claude asks to work inside your folder, press yes. That is all there is to it. Tomorrow we look at why 'make it better' is the worst instruction you can give a builder.

cards.body: Tonight: make a folder called hello, start claude inside it, and ask for a page that shows today's date in big letters and opens in your browser. Then ask for one change.
cards.simpler: Tonight, try it yourself. Make a folder called hello and start claude inside it. Ask for a page that shows today's date in big letters and opens in your browser. When it appears, ask for **one change**, like a different colour or bigger text, and watch the page catch up.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now start Claude Code inside a folder, ask for one small thing in plain English, and see it run in your browser.
